summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's institutional anti-LGBT posture has a documented origin point. In August 2016 the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities to be mental illnesses and recommended psychological "rehabilitation"; the Jokowi government remained mostly silent at the time.

Human Rights Watch has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016. Its 7 July 2026 report, "Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students", follows official condemnation of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organisation, documented 94 cases. In early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor their children in relation to what they described as a lifestyle.

The escalation described by The Diplomat and ABC News is presented as continuous rather than sudden: analysts state that attacks on trans women did not suddenly appear, and trace the current surge to officials' verbal attacks and to the October 2025 defence decree.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal recognition of a same-sex partner, since same-sex marriage is not permitted, and are exposed to the penal code's extra-marital sex provision regardless of where the conduct occurs. Selective prosecution means exposure is shaped by complaint, publicity and local official priorities rather than by a fixed charging practice.

Risk attaches to private gatherings as well as public visibility. The Puncak villa raid of June 2025 targeted a rented private venue with no lawful basis according to Amnesty International, indicating that residents hosting or attending private social events face arrest.

Trans and gender-nonconforming residents also face pathologisation in official health frameworks following the Indonesian Psychiatric Association's 2016 classification of transgender identity as mental illness and its recommendation of rehabilitation. Students are a documented target of abuse, and officials have publicly urged families to supervise children associated with LGBT people.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of the October 2025 presidential decree is not resolved here. The sources describe it as framing LGBTQ+ people within national defence doctrine and as encouraging official and vigilante hostility; none of them records a prosecution or administrative action brought against an individual under the decree itself.

Enforcement of the same-sex provisions recorded for South Sumatra is not evidenced in these sources. The Human Dignity Trust profile states that the provisions exist, but no recent case from that province is documented here, so the practical enforcement picture outside Aceh remains unresolved.

The reported demand of up to US$100,000 in the Ventocilla case rests on the family's account of a WhatsApp call and is not independently corroborated in the sources available; the police position in that case is a denial of violence rather than a response to the payment demand.

Quantitative totals for vigilante attacks on trans women following the October 2025 decree are not established by these sources. Reporting characterises a clear surge and names the decree as a contributing cause, but the aggregate count and its geographic spread are unresolved.
